1A.title: Questions and answers
words: Too interested in other people’s private lives
A person who applies for a job
A document with your education and work history
The money you earn from your job
A question that asks for more details
A feeling you can’t explain; intuition
Making you feel shy or stupid
Cannot fail; very easy to use
A person who loves computers or technology
Time for your job vs time for your life
The person who asks the questions
Wanting to know or learn things

g.title: Question formation
g.rule:
Good questions follow a few fixed patterns.

auxiliary before the subjectHow long have you worked here? · Why didn't she call?
subject questions: no do / didWho told you? · What happened?
preposition at the endWhat are you thinking about? · Who did you go with?
indirect questions: normal word orderCould you tell me where the office is? · Do you know if he has left?

ex.q: Could you tell me what time ___?
Who ___ this report?
What are you waiting ___?

talk: Interview your partner for a job they would love. Ask at least six questions.
What is the strangest question you have ever been asked?

l.intro: Two friends compare job interviews.

script.t: Manneh, how did the interview go? Who interviewed you?
The head of the department. She asked me what I would do if I were an animal.
Seriously? What did you answer?
I said a dolphin. Then she wanted to know why I had left my last job.
That's a fair question. Did she ask about salary?
No, but she asked how I felt about my work–life balance, which seemed a bit nosy.
Do you know whether you got it?
Not yet. My gut feeling is good, though. The small talk at the end went well.
Could you tell me who else applied?
Forty applicants, apparently. I sent a follow-up email this morning.

ex.q: Who interviewed Manneh?
Which question did he find nosy?
Manneh already knows that he got the job.
What did he do this morning?

1B.title: It’s a mystery
words: A person who says they can see the future
Two similar things happen by chance at the same time
Information that helps solve a mystery
An idea that tries to explain something
Nice to your face, nasty behind your back
A person who reads your future in cards or palms

g.title: Auxiliary verbs; the…, the… + comparatives
g.rule:
Auxiliaries do a lot of work in conversation.

short answers and echo questionsI've seen a ghost. — Have you?
So / Neither + auxiliarySo do I. · Neither have I.
emphasisI do believe you. · She did call, I promise.
the + comparative, the + comparativeThe more I read about it, the less I understand.

ex.q: You believe in coincidences, ___?
The longer I waited, ___ I became.
I didn't see anything strange. — Neither ___ I.

talk: Describe something that happened to you which you can't explain.
Do you believe some people can predict the future? Why or why not?

l.intro: A sceptic and a believer discuss a strange evening.

script.t: Rosa, you don't really believe that psychic, do you?
I do, actually. She knew my grandmother's name.
Did she? You probably mentioned it yourself.
I didn't. And she said I'd get a phone call, and I did, an hour later.
That's a coincidence. The more people she sees, the more often she's right.
You're so sceptical. Have you never had a spooky experience?
I have, actually. But there's always a theory that explains it.
So do I have no evidence?
None. And the longer you talk to her, the more clues you give her.
Well, I'm not superstitious, but I'm going back next week.

ex.q: What did the psychic know?
Daniyar thinks the phone call was a coincidence.
According to Daniyar, why is the psychic often right?
o: She sees a lot of people

ex.q: What is Rosa going to do?

2A.title: Doctor, doctor!
words: A sign that you are ill
To hurt a joint by twisting it
Someone who always thinks they are ill
A painful bubble on your skin from shoes
To lose consciousness for a short time
A long piece of cloth to wrap an injury
Your body reacts badly to something

g.title: Present perfect simple and continuous
g.rule:
Both link the past to now; the choice depends on your focus.

result, a completed action, how manyI've seen the doctor twice this month.
activity, how long, a recent activity with a visible resultI've been feeling dizzy all week. · You've been running.
non-action verbs → simpleI've had this cough for ages.

ex.q: How long ___ these tablets?
I ___ three appointments this week.
She ___ (know) her doctor since she was a child.

talk: Have you or someone you know ever had an accident or an injury? What happened?
What have you been doing recently to stay healthy?

l.intro: A customer asks a pharmacist for advice.

script.t: Good morning. How can I help?
I've been feeling dizzy since Monday, and I've got a rash on my arm.
Have you taken anything for it?
I've taken two painkillers a day, but they haven't helped.
Have you been eating anything unusual?
Now you mention it, I've been trying a new diet. And I've had food poisoning twice this year.
I think you should have a check-up. Have you seen your doctor?
Not yet. My wife says I'm a hypochondriac. I've already been to the surgery four times this month.
Even so, a rash and dizziness together need a proper look.
All right. I've been putting it off for too long.

ex.q: How long has the customer been feeling dizzy?
The painkillers have helped.
What does the pharmacist recommend?
What does his wife call him?

2B.title: Act your age
words: Differences between young and old people
Not working any more because of age
Someone the same age as you
Wear smart clothes for a special event

g.title: Using adjectives as nouns; adjective order
g.rule:
Two things to know about adjectives.

the + adjective = a group of peoplethe young · the elderly · the unemployed (plural verb)
nationalitiesthe French · the Japanese; but the Italians, the Kazakhs
order: opinion → size → age → colour → origin → materiala lovely long black Italian leather coat

ex.q: ___ often have more free time than people who work.
She was wearing a ___ dress.
The young ___ (be) more worried about climate change.

talk: Should people dress their age? Describe what you think suits different generations.
Describe the clothes of someone whose style you admire.

l.intro: A mother and her daughter argue about clothes.

script.t: Arman, you're not going to the interview in that scruffy hoodie, are you?
It's a nice grey cotton hoodie, Mum. The young don't wear suits any more.
The middle-aged do. And the interviewer is fifty.
That's the generation gap. You think trendy means untidy.
I think a smart dark blue jacket never looks old-fashioned.
The rich can afford jackets like that.
There's a lovely old Italian wool one in your father's wardrobe.
Dad's? It's enormous. And striped.
Try it. The retired know a few things about first impressions.
Fine. But I'm keeping my denim shirt.

ex.q: What does Arman want to wear?
What does his mother suggest?
Arman thinks young people still wear suits.
What will Arman keep?

lessons.title: Using adjectives as nouns; adjective order

3A.title: Fasten your seat belts
words: Where you show your boarding pass and get on the plane
Tiredness after a long flight across time zones
The people who look after passengers on a plane
Sudden, bumpy movement of the plane
A seat next to the passage between the rows
Where you collect your suitcase after landing
The document that lets you get on the plane
Show your ticket and give your bags to the airline
When a plane leaves the ground
A flight over a very long distance
The cupboard above your seat for bags
Where officers check what you bring into a country
The space for your legs in front of your seat

g.title: Narrative tenses, past perfect continuous; so / such…that
g.rule:
A good story uses four past forms.

main eventsWe boarded and the plane took off.
background in progressPeople were sleeping when the turbulence began.
earlier action · earlier activity in progressThe pilot had warned us. · We had been flying for six hours.
so + adjective · such + (a) nounIt was so frightening that I couldn't speak. · It was such a long flight that I read two books.

ex.q: We ___ for an hour when the announcement was made.
It was ___ bad weather that the airport closed.
When I got to the gate, the flight ___ (already / leave).

talk: Tell the story of your best or worst journey by air, train or bus.
Are you a nervous traveller? What helps you?

l.intro: A traveller tells a colleague about a difficult journey.

script.t: Kate, you look exhausted. Didn't you sleep on the plane?
Not a minute. We'd been waiting at the gate for three hours when they finally let us board.
Why the delay?
The cabin crew hadn't arrived. Then, just as we were taking off, a storm started.
Was there turbulence?
It was so bad that the drinks flew off the trays. The man in the aisle seat was praying.
And when you landed?
My suitcase had been sent to another city. I'd been standing at baggage reclaim for an hour before they told me.
It was such a terrible trip that you deserve a day off.
Tell that to my jet lag.

ex.q: How long did the passengers wait at the gate?
Why was the flight delayed?
Kate's suitcase arrived with her.
How does Kate feel now?

lessons.title: Narrative tenses, past perfect continuous; so / such…that
Listening: The worst flight of my life

3B.title: A really good ending?
words: An unexpected change at the end of a story
An ending that leaves you in suspense
The events that happen in a story
A book about a real person’s life
In the end, after a long time
In the main and most important way
Finally, after a series of events

g.title: The position of adverbs and adverbial phrases
g.rule:
Where an adverb goes depends on its type.

manner, place, time: usually at the endShe read the story quickly. · We met at the library last week.
frequency and degree: before the main verb, after beI hardly ever finish a novel. · It is incredibly short.
comment adverbs: at the beginningUnfortunately, the ending was predictable.

ex.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: I read always the last page first.
I always read the last page first.
Always I read the last page first.

ex.q: ___, nobody knew how the story would end.
He speaks English very ___ (good).

talk: Tell the plot of a short story, film or series in two minutes. Do you like the ending?
Do you ever read the last page of a book first? Why or why not?

l.intro: Two friends talk about a novel they are both reading.

script.t: Luke, have you finished the book yet?
Nearly. Apparently there's a twist in the last chapter.
Don't tell me! I've only just started it.
I won't. Basically, the plot moves very slowly at first.
I noticed. I almost gave up after fifty pages.
Gradually it gets better. Eventually you can't put it down.
Ideally, I'd read it in one weekend.
Then stay off the internet. People carelessly post the ending everywhere.
Honestly, I prefer a predictable story to a ruined one.
You'll never guess this one. Every chapter ends on a cliffhanger.

ex.q: Dina has almost finished the book.
How does the plot move at first?
What advice does Luke give?
How does every chapter end?

lessons.title: The position of adverbs and adverbial phrases
Listening: Don't tell me the ending

4A.title: Stormy weather
words: A long period with little or no rain
A snowstorm with very strong winds
A period of unusually hot weather
Pollution in city air that makes it hard to see
Small balls of ice that fall like rain
Warm and wet, but not raining
When everything is covered with water
A violent storm with very strong winds
A flash of very bright light in the sky
Energy that will not run out, e.g. solar

g.title: Future perfect and future continuous
g.rule:
Look at the future from a point in the future.

finished before a future time → will have + past participleBy 2050, sea levels will have risen.
in progress at a future time → will be + -ingThis time next week I'll be skiing.
time expressionsby Friday · by the time you arrive · in ten years' time

ex.q: By the end of this year, I ___ my degree.
Don't call at eight. We ___ dinner.
In twenty years' time, most cars ___ (be) electric.

talk: What will you be doing this time next year? What will you have done by then?
How do you think the climate will have changed your region by 2050?

l.intro: A radio presenter interviews a climate scientist.

script.t: Dr Ospanova, what will our summers be like in thirty years?
By 2050, average temperatures will have risen by about two degrees.
And what will that mean day to day?
We'll be having longer heatwaves, and farmers will be facing regular droughts.
Will winters disappear?
No, but blizzards will be rarer. Instead, it'll be pouring with rain more often.
Will we have stopped using fossil fuels by then?
I hope we will have replaced most of them. Otherwise smog will be getting worse in the cities.
Are you optimistic?
Cautiously. In ten years' time most new cars will be eco-friendly.

ex.q: By how much will temperatures have risen by 2050?
What will farmers be facing?
The scientist says blizzards will be more common.
How does she describe herself?

4B.title: A risky business
words: A person who likes doing dangerous or exciting things
The excited feeling in your body when you’re scared
Jumping from a plane with a parachute
Jumping from a bridge on an elastic rope
Insurance you buy before a trip
To look or behave like an older family member
To look after someone or something
Flying through the air in a special suit
Brave enough to do dangerous things

g.title: Zero and first conditionals, future time clauses
g.rule:
Use these for real situations.

always true → zero: if + present, presentIf you heat ice, it melts.
possible future → first: if + present, will / may / can / imperativeIf you don't wear a helmet, you'll get hurt.
time clauses + present, not willI'll text you as soon as I land. · Wait until it has stopped.
in caseTake a jacket in case it gets cold.

ex.q: I'll tell you as soon as I ___ any news.
Take your phone ___ you get lost.
You won't improve unless you ___ (practise).

talk: Are you a risk-taker? Talk about a risk you took and one you would never take.
What safety advice would you give a tourist visiting your country?

l.intro: An instructor prepares a nervous customer for a bungee jump.

script.t: Right. If you listen carefully, nothing will go wrong.
What happens if the rope breaks?
It doesn't. If a rope is used two hundred times, we replace it.
Should I close my eyes?
If you close them, you'll miss the best part. Take your time.
I'm not really a risk-taker. I take after my mother.
Don't jump until I say so. As soon as you hear three, lean forward.
Have you got my travel insurance details in case something happens?
Yes. Unless you tell me to stop, I'll start counting.
OK. If I survive, I'll take up something quieter. Like chess.

ex.q: When is a rope replaced?
The instructor tells him to close his eyes.
When should he lean forward?
What will he take up if he survives?

lessons.title: Zero and first conditionals, future time clauses

5A.title: I’m a survivor
words: A large mass of snow falling down a mountain
A simple structure that protects you from bad weather
A person who enters a building illegally
Sad because you are away from home
Happy because a worry or problem has gone
So surprised you cannot move or react
With little hope and ready to do anything
Feeling such strong emotions you do not know how to react
Bored or annoyed with something that has continued too long
Upset because someone was rude or ignored you
Continuing to live in a dangerous situation

g.title: Unreal conditionals
g.rule:
Use these to imagine a different present or past.

second: if + past, would + verbIf I were lost in a forest, I'd follow a river.
third: if + past perfect, would have + past participleIf they had taken a map, they wouldn't have got lost.
mixedIf I had listened, I wouldn't be here now.

ex.q: If I ___ what to do, I would have helped.
If we had more water, we ___ so worried.
If she hadn't called for help, she ___ (not / survive).

talk: How would you cope if you were lost somewhere wild for three days?
Tell a survival story you have read or seen. What would you have done?

l.intro: Two colleagues discuss a survival story in the news.

script.t: Did you read about the skier who survived the avalanche?
Yes. If he hadn't built a shelter, he would have frozen.
I'd have panicked. If I were buried in snow, I wouldn't know what to do.
Apparently he stayed calm. If he had tried to walk, he'd have got lost.
His family must have been desperate.
They were stunned when he phoned. If his battery had died, nobody would have found him.
Would you go skiing there now?
Only if I had a guide. I'd be homesick after one night alone.
If I'd been him, I'd never ski again.
He says he's going back next winter.

ex.q: How did the skier survive?
He tried to walk out and got lost.
How did his family feel when he phoned?
What is he going to do next winter?

lessons.title: Listening: What would you have done?

5B.title: Wish you were here
words: A feeling of sadness about something you did or did not do
Annoyed because you cannot do or change something
Making you feel silly in front of others
Making you want to do something great
Sad because something was not as good as you hoped
Rude in a way that upsets people
The quality of telling the truth
Showing a lot of interest and excitement
When someone says no to you or does not accept you

g.title: wish for present / future; wish for past regrets
g.rule:
After wish, go one tense back from the real situation.

present → wish + pastI wish I had more time. · I wish I could drive.
annoying habits → wish + wouldI wish you wouldn't interrupt.
past regrets → wish + past perfectI wish I had studied harder.
If only = strongerIf only I hadn't said that.

ex.q: I wish I ___ so much last night.
I wish my neighbours ___ so much noise.
If only I ___ (can) speak three languages.

talk: What do you regret doing or not doing? What do you wish were different now?
What habits of other people annoy you? I wish people wouldn't…

l.intro: Two friends talk about regrets.

script.t: Chris, do you have any regrets?
Plenty. I wish I'd learned to play an instrument as a child.
It's not too late. I wish I had more free time, though.
I wish my boss wouldn't email me at midnight. It's infuriating.
Mine does too. If only I hadn't accepted that promotion.
Really? I thought you found it inspiring.
At first. Now it's just exhausting. I wish I could go back to my old team.
I wish I'd travelled before I started working.
If only we were twenty again.
Honestly? I wouldn't change much. I just wish I worried less.

ex.q: What does Chris wish he had learned?
What annoys Chris about his boss?
Madina is happy she accepted the promotion.
What does Madina wish in the end?

lessons.title: wish for present / future; wish for past regrets
Listening: I wish I hadn't said that

6A.title: Night night
words: Open your mouth wide because you are tired
A short sleep during the day
Breathe noisily while you are asleep
The soft thing you put your head on in bed
A thick soft bed cover filled with feathers
Thin cloth covers on a bed
A warm cover for a bed, often made of wool
Someone who wakes up very easily
Prepare a clock to wake you up
Tiredness after flying to a different time zone

g.title: used to, be used to, get used to
g.rule:
Three forms that look similar and mean different things.

past habit, not true nowI used to sleep eight hours.
be used to + noun / -ing = it is normal for meI'm used to working nights.
get used to + noun / -ing = it is becoming normalI can't get used to getting up at five.

ex.q: I ___ wake up early, but now I get up at six every day.
It took me months to ___ the noise.
She's used to ___ (sleep) with the window open.

talk: How have your sleeping habits changed since you were a child?
Describe something new you had to get used to. How long did it take?

l.intro: A nurse talks about working night shifts.

script.t: How long have you been working nights?
Two years. I used to sleep eight hours without a problem.
And now?
I'm used to sleeping during the day, but it took months.
What was hardest to get used to?
Eating dinner at three in the morning. I still can't get used to that.
Do you ever oversleep?
I used to, so now I have three alarms. And I take a short nap before work.
Would you go back to days?
I'm so used to the quiet that I'd probably miss it. I don't even yawn any more.

ex.q: How long has the nurse worked nights?
She found it easy to get used to sleeping during the day.
What can't she get used to?
o: Eating dinner at three in the morning

ex.q: What does she do before work?

lessons.title: used to, be used to, get used to

6B.title: Music to my ears
words: A person who directs an orchestra
A group of people who sing together
A large group of classical musicians
A woman with the highest singing voice
A large string instrument you play sitting down
A wind instrument you hold sideways
A curved wind instrument popular in jazz
One more song at the end of a concert
A type or style of music, film, or book
A regular pattern of beats in music
A list of songs to play one after another
A person who makes coffee in a café
A person whose job is to drive someone’s car

g.title: Gerunds and infinitives
g.rule:
The first verb decides; a few verbs change meaning.

+ -ingenjoy, avoid, can't stand, keep, miss, suggest
+ toafford, agree, manage, refuse, tend, pretend
remember / forgetI remember hearing it (memory). · Remember to practise (don't forget).
stop · tryI stopped playing (gave up). · I stopped to listen (in order to). · Try turning it up (experiment).

ex.q: I'll never forget ___ that song for the first time.
He stopped ___ the piano when he was ten.
We can't afford ___ (go) to the concert.

talk: What music do you remember loving as a child? What do you tend to listen to now?
Does music change your mood? Give examples.

l.intro: Two parents talk after a concert.

script.t: Erlan, did you enjoy the concert?
I did. I'll never forget hearing my daughter play the cello on stage.
She was wonderful. My son forgot to bring his flute.
Oh no. Did he manage to borrow one?
Yes, but he kept stopping to check the music.
The choir was excellent. Do you remember singing in one at school?
I do. I tried to learn the saxophone too, but I gave up practising.
You should try taking lessons again.
I can't afford to buy a saxophone. Maybe I'll stop making excuses, though.
The orchestra needs adults. Remember to ask the conductor.

ex.q: What does Erlan's daughter play?
What did Laura's son forget?
Laura still plays the saxophone.
Who should Laura ask about the orchestra?

7A.title: Let’s not argue
words: Speak angrily to someone because you disagree
Say that something is not true
Say you will not do something
Give something that the person will give back
Take something that you will give back
Understand or become aware of something
Take money from a person or bank by force
Tell someone that something bad may happen
A list of jobs that people take turns to do
A person you share a flat with

g.title: Past modals: must have, etc.; would rather
g.rule:
Use modal + have + past participle to speculate about or criticise the past.

sure it happened · sure it didn'tShe must have forgotten. · He can't have meant it.
perhapsThey might have had an argument.
criticismYou should have told me. · You shouldn't have shouted.
would ratherI'd rather not talk about it. · I'd rather you didn't shout.

ex.q: He isn't answering. He ___ his phone at home.
You ___ that. It really hurt her.
I'd rather you ___ (not / tell) anyone.

talk: Describe an argument you had or saw. What should the people have done differently?
What do couples or flatmates most often argue about?

l.intro: Two flatmates work out what happened.

script.t: Asel, the front door was open when I got home. You must have forgotten to lock it.
I can't have. I left at seven and I checked it twice.
Then Dana might have come back for something.
She can't have. She's been in Astana since Monday.
Well, somebody must have opened it. Is anything missing?
My laptop is here. The wind might have pushed it open.
You should have told the landlord about that lock.
I did! He should have fixed it weeks ago.
I'd rather not argue. Let's call him now.
I'd rather you called him. He never denies anything to you.

ex.q: What was wrong when Jack got home?
Dana might have opened the door.
What do they think might have opened it?
Who is going to call the landlord?

lessons.title: Past modals: must have, etc.; would rather
Listening: Who left the door open?

7B.title: It’s all an act
words: Close one eye quickly as a signal
Look at something for a long time
Move your eyebrows together because you are angry or worried
Move your hand to say hello or goodbye
Rub your skin with your nails
The joint between your hand and your arm
The joint between your foot and your leg
The lines of hair above your eyes
Lines on your skin when you get older
Short hair on a man’s face after a day or two
The part of your face above your eyes
What your movements and face show about your feelings

g.title: Verbs of the senses
g.rule:
After look, feel, smell, sound, taste the pattern depends on what follows.

+ adjectiveYou look tired. · It sounds great.
+ like + nounShe looks like her mother. · It tastes like chicken.
+ as if / as though + clauseHe looks as if he hasn't slept.

ex.q: That actor ___ a real doctor.
You sound ___ you have a cold.
This fabric ___ (feel) really soft.

talk: Can you tell what a person is feeling from their body language? Give examples.
Describe an actor's performance that impressed you.

l.intro: An acting teacher gives feedback to a student.

script.t: That was better, but you still look as if you're reading the lines.
It feels natural to me.
It sounds flat. When you say sorry, you should look as though you mean it.
How? Should I frown?
Try a small shrug first. Then look at her. Don't stare.
Like this?
Yes. Now you look like a real person. Your voice sounds warmer too.
It feels strange to wave at nobody.
It looks right from here. And don't scratch your wrist. You seem nervous.
I am nervous. Does it look that obvious?

ex.q: What is the teacher's first criticism?
o: He looks as if he's reading the lines

ex.q: What does she tell him to try first?
The teacher tells him to stare at the other actor.
What makes him seem nervous?

8A.title: Cutting crime
words: A person who breaks into a house to steal
A person who attacks people in the street to take their money
A person who gets into computer systems illegally
Asking for money so you won’t tell a secret
Giving money to get an official to help you
Taking a person and asking for money
Taking goods into a country illegally
Twelve people who decide if someone is guilty
The person who controls a trial and decides the punishment
A person who saw a crime
The decision: guilty or not guilty
Found not guilty and allowed to go free
Information that shows if something is true
A dishonest trick to get money

g.title: The passive (all forms); have something done; it is said that…
g.rule:
Three ways to move the focus away from the doer.

all tensesHe is being questioned. · The car had been stolen. · It will be found.
have + object + past participle (someone does it for you)We had an alarm installed.
formal reportingIt is said that he escaped. · He is believed to be abroad.

ex.q: The suspect ___ by police at the moment.
We ___ last week.
o: had changed our locks by someone

ex.q: The thieves are thought ___ (be) professionals.

talk: What can people do to protect their homes and phones from crime?
Describe a crime that was in the news. What is said to have happened?

l.intro: A newsreader and a reporter cover a crime story.

script.t: A valuable painting has been stolen from the city gallery. Our reporter is there.
Thank you. The painting is believed to have been taken at about three this morning.
Has anyone been arrested?
Not yet. The cameras had been switched off, and it is thought that the burglars had inside help.
Is the gallery being searched?
Yes, staff are being questioned as we speak. The alarm is said to have been repaired only last week.
How much is the painting worth?
It is estimated to be worth two million. The gallery had its security checked in May.
Could it be an insurance fraud?
That hasn't been ruled out. A reward will be offered tomorrow.

ex.q: When was the painting taken?
o: At about three in the morning

ex.q: Someone has already been arrested.
What do police think about the burglars?
What will happen tomorrow?

lessons.title: The passive (all forms); have something done; it is said that…

8B.title: Fake news
words: The title at the top of a news story
A newspaper with short articles and lots of photos
The person in charge of a newspaper
A person who collects and reports news
A person who reads the news on TV or radio
A person who describes a sports event as it happens
A person who gives advice to readers in a magazine
Based only on facts, not feelings
Making a story more shocking than it is
With some information removed by an authority
False stories that look like real news
Say that you did not do something
Make someone agree to do something

g.title: Reporting verbs
g.rule:
Instead of said, use a verb that shows what the speaker was doing.

+ to + verbagree, offer, refuse, promise, threaten
+ person + to + verbadvise, persuade, remind, warn, invite
+ -ingadmit, deny, suggest, recommend

talk: How do you decide whether a news story is true?

l.intro: A journalism teacher talks to a student about a story.

script.t: Zhanna, where did this headline come from?
A tabloid. It accuses the mayor of taking a bribe.
Has he denied doing it?
Yes. He insists on seeing the evidence, and he's threatened to sue.
Did the reporter admit inventing anything?
No, but a colleague advised me not to trust the source.
Good advice. I'd recommend calling the mayor's office yourself.
They refused to comment yesterday.
Then remind them that we want to be objective. A biased story helps nobody.
I'll try again. I promised to finish it by Friday.

ex.q: Where did the headline come from?
What has the mayor threatened to do?
The mayor's office gave a comment yesterday.

Exciting, but the traffic is terrible and public transport is overcrowded.

l.intro: A school group visits a research laboratory.

script.t: Welcome. Every experiment in this laboratory is recorded on camera.
Do all the scientists work on the same project?
No. Most of us study sleep, and both of my assistants study memory.
Are any of the experiments dangerous?
None of them are. Neither of the two machines over there uses radiation.
Do you test on people?

Either a headache or nothing at all. All of them recover in an hour.
